\chapter*{Portuguese pronunciation --- a reference}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{Portuguese pronunciation (reference)}
\markboth{Pronunciation}{Pronunciation}

A \textbf{reference}, not a chapter — each lesson gives the sounds its word needs; this page gathers them. Portuguese spelling is fairly regular, but its \textbf{nasal vowels} and soft consonants surprise English speakers.

\section*{The traps for an English speaker}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \textbf{Nasal vowels.} A vowel before \emph{m/n} (or under a tilde \textasciitilde{}) goes through the nose: \emph{bom} = \emph{bõ}, \emph{sim} (\textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{}) = \emph{sĩ}, \emph{pão} (\textquotedblleft{}bread\textquotedblright{}) = \emph{pãw}. English has no exact match — hum the vowel.
  \item \textbf{Vowels reduce.} Unstressed \emph{e} often fades to a whisper or \emph{i}; final \emph{o} sounds like \emph{u} (\emph{obrigado} $\approx$ \textquotedblleft{}oh-bree-GAH-doo\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{s} between vowels = \emph{z}; at a syllable's end, often \emph{sh} (European Portuguese) or \emph{s} (most of Brazil).
  \item \textbf{lh} = the \emph{lli} of \emph{million}; \textbf{nh} = the \emph{ny} of \emph{canyon}; \textbf{ç} = \emph{s}.
  \item \textbf{r/rr} at word-start or doubled is a strong guttural (like a Scottish/French \emph{r} or even an \emph{h}); a single \emph{r} between vowels is a light tap.
\end{itemize}

\section*{Stress}

Usually the second-to-last syllable; a written accent (\emph{á}, \emph{â}, \emph{ã}, \emph{é}, \emph{ê}) marks any exception (\emph{olá}, \emph{café}, \emph{avô}).

\section*{Portuguese in the Romance family}

Portuguese, Spanish, French, and Italian are all worn-down Latin. Portuguese often eroded the most (the article \emph{ille} $\to$ \emph{o}); it turned Latin \emph{-ct-} into \emph{-it-} (\emph{noite}, like French \emph{nuit}); and it kept \emph{dies} close (\emph{o dia}, like Spanish \emph{día}). The lessons draw these contrasts as they arise.
